title: Illness on the oracle bones

confidence.note: The inscriptions belong to the Late Shang court at Anyang, conventionally dated c. 1250–1050 BCE; the toothache series falls in King Wu Ding's reign, whose exact years are themselves estimates. Readings of some body-part characters are debated, and translations differ over which ancestor was blamed for the king's tooth.

people: Wu Ding (reigned c. 1254–1197 BCE), Shang king whose ailments were divined
summary: China's oldest writing includes a king's toothache: Shang diviners cracked bones to learn which dead ancestor was causing it.
body: Some of the oldest Chinese writing is about being ill. On turtle shells and animal shoulder blades, diviners at the Late Shang court (c. 1250–1050 BCE) put questions to the royal ancestors about "affliction" in the bodies of the king and his family: head, eyes, ears, teeth, abdomen and more. When King Wu Ding had a sick tooth, a series of divinations tried to identify which dead relative was causing it, so that the right one could be appeased with sacrifice. The bones record exorcism and offerings, not drugs. Skeletons from Anyang show why teeth mattered: cavities, abscesses and gum disease were widespread.

links.note: A thousand years later, recipes and cautery appear beside spells.

title: The Mawangdui medical manuscripts

confidence.note: The burial date of 168 BCE is firm, but it is only the latest possible date for the texts: their script suggests many were copied in the Qin dynasty (221–206 BCE), and some works may be older still. Counts of texts and recipes vary slightly with how fragments are grouped.

people: Li Xi (d. 168 BCE), nobleman, probably the occupant of tomb 3
summary: A lacquer box buried in 168 BCE held medicine before acupuncture: eleven body vessels, burning moxa, and hundreds of recipes mixed with spells.
body: In 168 BCE a nobleman in his early thirties, probably Li Xi of the family of Li Cang, a local lord of the Changsha kingdom, was buried at Mawangdui in what is now Changsha, Hunan, with a lacquer box of about thirty manuscripts on silk and bamboo. When tomb 3 was opened in the early 1970s, sixteen of them turned out to be medical. Along with texts from a slightly earlier tomb at Zhangjiashan, they transformed what historians knew about early Chinese medicine.

The manuscripts describe eleven "vessels" running through the body, each tied to its own ailments, and treat them by cauterizing with burning moxa. There are no acupuncture points and no needling, and not yet the twelve channels of the later *Inner Classic*. The longest text, *Recipes for Fifty-Two Ailments*, holds some 283 remedies for 103 conditions, alongside lancing of swellings and incantations in which the healer threatens harmful spirits with a beating. Drugs, cautery and magic sat side by side.

links.note: Its eleven vessels grew into the twelve channels of the Inner Classic.
Ancestors and exorcism, a millennium earlier.

title: The Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic

date.display: c. 3rd century BCE – 2nd century CE (core); reshaped to the 11th century

confidence.note: A Chinese national nomination to UNESCO dates the core to the Warring States period; Unschuld places its origins in short essays of the final centuries BCE; others argue the received text is largely Tang material edited in the Song. All agree it is anonymous, composite and heavily re-edited, and that its attribution to the Yellow Emperor is legend.

people: Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor, legendary sage-ruler to whom it is attributed
Paul U. Unschuld, modern historian and translator of the Suwen and Lingshu
summary: The founding classic of Chinese medicine is credited to a legendary emperor. In fact it was written by many hands and reworked for a thousand years.
body: No book has shaped Chinese medicine more than the *Huangdi neijing*, the *Inner Classic of the Yellow Emperor*. It survives as two books: the *Suwen* (*Plain Questions*), mostly on cosmological theory, and the *Lingshu* (*Divine Pivot*), mostly on needling. Knowledge passes in question and answer, with the Yellow Emperor as the ruler who asks and sage advisers such as Qi Bo as the experts who explain.

Its body is a web of correspondences. Health depends on the proper flow of *qi* along channels linked to the organs, in step with yin and yang, the five phases, the seasons and the hours. Illness comes when "perverse *qi*" such as wind, heat or cold invades. Treatment works on twelve channels with needles and moxa, alongside advice on diet and on living in harmony with the surroundings.

When was it written? Tradition credits the Yellow Emperor himself. China's nomination of a 1339 printed edition to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register dates the core to the Warring States period (475–221 BCE), with Qin and Han additions. Paul Unschuld traces the *Suwen* to many short essays written in the final centuries BCE to explain health through the newly developed vessel theory. Manuscripts buried at Mawangdui in 168 BCE know only eleven vessels and no needling, which suggests the system was still being assembled. A *Huangdi neijing* is listed in the Han imperial library catalogue, but the texts read today were rearranged and expanded for a millennium; the *Suwen* as now known emerged from 11th-century editing, and one recent survey describes it as mostly Tang material edited by Song scholars.

Its prestige ran ahead of its use. Unschuld argues that needling and the yin-yang and five-phase doctrines behind it remained a minority interest, kept alive by a few of the elite, until the 11th and 12th centuries, while drug remedies were the mainstay of everyday practice. Today the *Inner Classic* is treated as the founding text of traditional Chinese medicine, which gives the question of its age real weight.

myth.tradition: The Inner Classic preserves the teachings of the Yellow Emperor, a sage-ruler of remote antiquity, and is the oldest Chinese medical book.
myth.record: Huangdi is a legendary figure to whom Han-era writers attached many kinds of texts to lend them authority. The work is anonymous and composite, and medical manuscripts from tombs sealed in 186 and 168 BCE are older than any securely dated version of it.

title: The Divine Farmer's Materia Medica

confidence.note: No dated copy survives: Unschuld places its writing between the 1st century BCE and the 1st century CE, while other scholars say Eastern Han (25–220 CE). The original is lost, so its exact contents are known only through later editions and modern reconstructions.

people: Shennong, the Divine Farmer, legendary culture hero to whom it is attributed
Tao Hongjing (452/456–536), Daoist scholar who edited and expanded it
summary: China's first book of drugs sorted 365 substances into rulers, officials and helpers. It was named for a legendary sage who tasted every plant.
body: Legend says Shennong, the Divine Farmer, pitied human suffering and tasted every kind of plant, meeting a hundred poisons a day. The book that bears his name is far younger and anonymous: historians date it to the Han period, between the 1st century BCE and the 2nd century CE. It is the earliest known Chinese *bencao*, or materia medica, a book that describes drugs one by one instead of listing mixed recipes.

It covers 365 substances, the number of days in a year, for reasons no one has explained. Most are plants. They are sorted into three ranks that mirror the imperial court. Upper-rank "rulers" were nonpoisonous and helped prolong life; lower-rank "helpers" and "agents" carried poison and drove out disease; middle-rank "officials" sat between. Whether a drug "has poison" became a basic question in Chinese pharmacy.

The original is lost. Around 500 CE the Daoist scholar Tao Hongjing kept its three-part structure, added 365 further drugs, and launched the main line of Chinese drug books. The versions read today are reconstructions made by Chinese and Japanese scholars since the 17th century.

myth.tradition: The sage-emperor Shennong tasted hundreds of plants in remote antiquity and set down what he learned in this book.
myth.record: Shennong is a legendary culture hero. The text is anonymous and was compiled in the Han period; tradition attached his name to give it authority.

title: Zhang Zhongjing's Treatise on Cold Damage

confidence.note: The date rests on Zhang's approximate lifetime (c. 142–220); no manuscript of his own survives. That he wrote a treatise later rebuilt by Wang Shuhe is accepted, but how closely the transmitted Shanghan lun matches his original is uncertain, since it passed through 3rd-century reconstruction and 11th-century editing.

people: Zhang Ji, known as Zhang Zhongjing (c. 142–220?), physician and author
Wang Shuhe (210–285), court physician who reconstructed the text
Lin Yi (fl. 1057–1068), Song editor of the medical classics
summary: A Han physician's book on fevers was lost, rebuilt, and edited again, yet became the backbone of Chinese prescribing.
body: Around 200 CE a physician named Zhang Ji, better known as Zhang Zhongjing, wrote the *Shanghan zabing lun*, a treatise on "cold damage" and miscellaneous disorders. Cold damage belonged to a newer way of thinking about illness: disease caused by harmful external *qi*, such as wind, heat or cold, entering the body. Zhang matched these illnesses with recipes for drug decoctions, drawing on an older recipe tradition that tomb manuscripts now reveal.

His book did not survive intact. In the 3rd century the physician Wang Shuhe rebuilt it from what remained as two works: the *Shanghan lun* (*Treatise on Cold Damage*) and the *Jingui yaolüe* (*Essential Prescriptions of the Golden Cabinet*). The versions read today owe much to the 11th-century Song editor Lin Yi, and some later formularies credited to Zhang were Song reinventions. Even so, Zhang is revered as one of the great physicians of the Chinese tradition, sometimes called the Hippocrates of China.

title: Hua Tuo and the legend of mafeisan

confidence.note: Hua Tuo is usually dated c. 140–208 CE, but everything known about his surgery comes from histories written decades to two centuries after his death. The formula of mafeisan is lost, and whether it could have produced true surgical anesthesia is debated.

summary: Two Chinese histories say a 2nd-century surgeon numbed patients with a drug dissolved in wine. The recipe is lost, and the story cannot be checked.
body: Hua Tuo, who died in 208 CE, is China's most famous ancient surgeon. Two histories, the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (3rd century) and the *Book of the Later Han* (5th century), say he gave patients a powder called *mafeisan* dissolved in wine and then operated on them, including on the internal organs. If so, he was performing surgery under anesthesia some 1,600 years before ether.

How much of this is history is hard to say. The accounts were written long after his death, he is said to have burned his own papers, and the recipe is lost. The name probably means "boiled hemp powder"; modern attempts to reconstruct it from medieval texts suggest aconite, a potent poison, but its real contents and effect are unknown. A work of his that the 4th-century writer Ge Hong reportedly preserved was later lost too.

The legend outlived the drug. In Japan, Hanaoka Seishū set out to recreate mafeisan and on 13 October 1804 performed a partial mastectomy on a 60-year-old woman under general anesthesia with his own herbal mixture.

myth.tradition: Hua Tuo carried out abdominal surgery under full general anesthesia with mafeisan around 200 CE.
myth.record: The story rests on histories written after his death; his writings and the formula are lost. He may well have used a numbing drug, but its composition and power cannot be verified.

title: Ge Hong's handbook for emergencies

confidence.note: Ge Hong's life (283–343, or 281–341 in some accounts) bounds the date, but the handbook survives only in Tao Hongjing's later edited version, so which passages are Ge Hong's own cannot always be told.

people: Ge Hong (283–343), Daoist scholar and alchemist
Tu Youyou, pharmacologist and 2015 Nobel laureate who drew on the handbook
summary: A Daoist alchemist's pocket book of emergency cures held an early account of smallpox, and a line about wormwood that led to a Nobel Prize.
body: Ge Hong (283–343), a southern Chinese scholar best known for his book on elixirs of immortality, also compiled a handbook of remedies for emergencies, *Recipes from Behind the Elbow*, a title evoking a book carried in the sleeve. It survives only as edited by Tao Hongjing. It contains what may be China's earliest mention of smallpox, recognized as contagious. One line, steep a handful of *qinghao* in water, wring out the juice and drink it, led Tu Youyou in 1971 to extract the plant without heat, a key step toward artemisinin.

links.note: Tu Youyou's cold-extraction idea came from this text.
